chapter_theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள், 3 of 21), mostly short and grouped in pairs or sets that share a closing refrain: the poet asks to be freed from the lure of women, from disease and from Death, and to sing and serve the feet; one song judges arguers and hoarders bound for Death's town, one is a love-lament, and one asks for the yoga that would bring back the departing breath.
structure_note: Songs sharing a final refrain: 1024 to 1027 (the gods freed from the asuras' prison), 1028 to 1030 (தேவ தேவ தேவாதி தேவப் பெருமாளே), 1031 and 1032 (the dancing peacock steed), 1033 and 1034 (devotees of blameless justice), 1035 and 1036 (the sword-fight with Sura). Disease is the subject of 1025 and 1027, Death of 1028 and 1034, the body of 1034 to 1036.

1022.reading: The poet confesses being entranced by bejewelled women, and also wandering with a cunning mind, trusting men without understanding and singing them as golden-handed great patrons, and asks to be told how to sing the lotus feet in fresh and fitting verse instead of living in lies. The praise names the green-cloud Vishnu who as Rama felled ten heads and twenty arms with one arrow, one who wandered singing sweet songs of wisdom in devotion at the feet of the dancer whom Vishnu and Brahma cannot grasp, the vel thrown at Sura, and the Velaikkaran of the hill of millet and bamboo pearls.
1022.nuance: அறிவிலாரைத் தேறிப் பொற்கை புகழ் பெரியராகப் பாடி: the poet confesses the court poet's sin of praising undeserving patrons as generous, and asks instead for song for the Lord. The figure who wanders singing ஞானப் பாடல் at the dancer's feet may be Murugan as Sambandar, but the text does not name him.

1023.reading: The poet describes women who price their musk-smeared breasts for coins and sell love on camphor-scented beds, and asks whether, caught in the net of their kohl eyes that outdo Kama's arrows and Yama himself, he must go deluded to ruin. The praise is a chain of epithets ending in -kara: the one with the holy name Chetti, the glorious thrower of the vel, who circled the world in a moment on the peacock, the bridegroom with red flowers on his chest, plunderer of the asura lord, guardian of the gods' king, rider of the elephant, giver of release, and the Velaikkaran of the pure hunters' daughter.
1023.nuance: முலையை விலை கூறிக் காசுக்கு அளவே: the price is stated outright. செட்டி எனும் ஒர் திருநாமக்கார: Murugan bears the name Chetti, the merchant, presumably from a guise taken to approach Valli; the song names the title, not the story. The -kara chain is a rhythmic device.

1024.reading: The poet asks whether, deluded by women whose eyes scorn Kama's arrows, caring for neither land, town, house, wealth, children, wife nor kin, and without true knowledge, he must search through seven births and fall into hell. The praise names the green peacock that pecks the dancing serpent, Murugan who stands so all may be saved where the Veda speaks silence, Valli's bridegroom in the hunters' field, and the one who cut the prison where the asuras held the gods and set them free.
1024.nuance: நாடு நகர் ... சுற்றம் இவை பேணா: the poet's fault includes neglecting worldly duties for women, not only neglecting God. ஆரணம் உரைக்கும் மோன கவிடத்தில் is unclear; it may mean the place of silence the Veda points to.

1025.reading: The poet asks that when disease of cold, phlegm, fever, wind and bile surrounds the body and brings the life to slip away, before he perishes in a sea of grief with father and children around him, Murugan think to come and give the feet that taught the Veda on earth. The praise names Murugan who comes daily on the peacock to those who pine in love, who taught the Veda to the deluded brahmins before Vishnu and Brahma, and who freed the gods.
1025.nuance: The diseases are named by the humoral scheme (வாதம், பித்தம், with சீதம் and மலம்). மாதர் மயலுற்று வாட ... வருவோனே: here the pining is of women in love with Murugan, a reversal of the poet's usual infatuation.

1026.reading: The poet asks not to wander in the delusion of peacock-like women whose eyes and breasts crush young men's strength, and that a mind which thinks on Murugan's name, with sin gone, come into his hands: Murugan is the great life of devotees who think of him with song, music, dance and devotion. The praise names the dancing peacock, the teacher of the Veda's word to Siva, and the hero who stood as the hunter girl's servant.
1026.nuance: பாடல் இசை மிக்க ஆடல்கொடு பத்தியோடு நினை பத்தர்: devotion is pictured as performance, song, music and dance, the setting the poet asks to join.

1027.reading: The poet lists the diseases (spirit possession, colic, fever, swelling, the great belly, cough, anaemia, leprosy, wind, bile and piles) and asks that none of them come near him as he wastes, and that he be set to live in the high state of release. The praise names Valli's husband, the peacock that measured the whole earth in its running, and Murugan who removes the sufferings of devotees who chant the Veda.
1027.nuance: The plea is a medical catalogue; the cure asked for is release (முத்தி நீடிய பதம்) rather than health alone.

1028.reading: Those who learn books to quarrel and win arguments, those who seek money and live without giving, and those who never melt saying 'life of the Lord who shares his body with the woman' all go to the town of great Death and wander there. The praise names Murugan the Lord of the form of nada who dwells in the heart, ruler of the serpent world and the fourteen worlds, bearer of the vel and the cock banner, God of the gods.
1028.nuance: The song has no plea: it is a judgement on three kinds of men, setting disputatious learning and ungiving wealth beside lovelessness. மாதுபாகர் வாழ்வே, the life of Siva the half-woman, is the address Murugan is given by those who do melt.

1029.reading: The song asks whether it is fitting that the girl, deluded by love, should waste away under Kama's arrows, the roaring sea, the cuckoo whose anger never ends and her own mother's harsh enmity. The praise names Murugan who rides the peacock in joy, the cock banner by which the seven worlds live, and the vel that fought Sura to ashes.
1029.nuance: An akam love-lament, not the poet's confession: the speaker (a companion, the mother or the girl herself; the text does not say) presents the classical afflictors of the lovesick girl, adding the mother's scolding (மாதாவின் வார்மைப் பகை).

1030.reading: The poet, who cannot speak truth while great craving remains, who suffered by joining ignorant women and learned only noisy books, a dog of a servant, asks Murugan to show him a little grace so that his life does not become empty chaff. The praise names him easy to reach for the bravest of heroes, the Kumara of the peacock, husband of the hunter creeper, and the steadfast God of gods.
1030.nuance: ஆவி சாவி யாகாமல்: சாவி is grain without a kernel, so the life is pictured as a husk. ஆரவாரம் மாறாத நூல்: learning that is only noise, as in 1028.

1031.reading: The poet, never sated by women's spear-eyes that reach their ears, their yazh-like speech, unseen waists, breasts and lips sweet as fresh cane juice, asks whether Murugan will not think even a little of letting him reach the meaning that no one can find by searching. The praise names Murugan the teacher of wisdom praised by Siva of the ash and his consort, the arms that embrace Valli, the vel that fought the mango tree and the hill in the sea, and the rider who makes the peacock dance as Sura's armies turn to dust.
1031.nuance: ஒருவர்க்கும் தேடொணாததொர் அர்த்தம்: the goal is a meaning beyond anyone's search, given only by grace. போத தேசிகன், the teacher of knowledge, is a title of Murugan here.

1032.reading: The poet asks Murugan to look on him so that, not infatuated with women's hair, eyes, lips, breasts and dancing feet, he may praise him with love. The praise names Murugan the child whom poets daily sing as 'Bala' and whose sorrow and sin he cuts away, giving the state of joy, son of Siva who bent Meru and wears the half moon, and the rider of the peacock while Kali dances in the blood sea of Sura's army.
1032.nuance: பாலகா என நித்தம் பாடு நாவலர்: the reward the praise names goes to poets who sing the god as a child, which is what the plea asks to become.

1033.reading: The poet asks not to wander in love with the sulking and noise of women whose eyes, brows and arms sell infatuation and make good men faint, and asks Murugan to understand him a little so that he may hold the feet that are his town, his mother and his kin. The praise names him the bridegroom of the girl on the hill who gave the hunters heaven, the one who speaks the name of safety kept by Siva, whom Vishnu and Brahma could not find, and the one who gives life to devotees of blameless justice.
1033.nuance: ஊர் பெற்ற தாய் சுற்றமாய் உற்ற தாள்: the feet take the place of home, mother and kin. ஊடற்குள்ளே புக்கு: the courtesan's sulk (ஊடல்) is a trap. Which name is meant in சேமத்தின் நாமத்தை மொழிவோனே is not said.

1034.reading: The poet asks that before the trident-bearer comes to seize the life from this hut of skin, bone and flesh, Murugan give him a mind keen in devotion to the flawless feet. The praise names the vel that struck down Sura who hid in the sea, Murugan who gave knowledge to the Primal one who swallowed the poison that would have killed the world and the gods, and the bridegroom of the doe-eyed girl.
1034.nuance: சூலத்தன்: here Death is the bearer of the trident, a weapon usually Siva's. The lines on the poison (ஆலத்தை ... ஆம் வித்தையாமத்தை அருள்வோனே) are compressed and their split into words is uncertain.

1035.reading: The poet, in a body of flesh with nine openings and a crore of womb-paths behind it, asks to sing Murugan's grace so as to grasp all learning and music, to seek his feet morning and evening without forgetting, and to worship the feet of those who praise his name. The praise names the vel by which the sun, moon, time, wind, cloud, sea, mountain and water, the gods who worship Siva's feet, Indra, Vishnu and Brahma live, and the sword-fight with Sura of many magics.
1035.nuance: நாமம் புகழ்பவர் பாதம் தொழ: the plea reaches beyond the Lord's feet to the devotees' feet. ஒன்பது வழி: the body's nine gates.

1036.reading: The poet, not knowing the strong act that ends the two karmas of this body of five elements bound as pasu and pasam, asks whether he will not attain the good yoga by which the little life that runs out in hundreds and thousands of breaths may be turned back. The praise names Valli of the millet field, the seas set on fire, the Vedas crying out, and the sword that cut Sura's chest and arms.
1036.nuance: அறுநூறும் பதினுறழ் நூறும் பதினிருபது நூறும் ஓடும் சிறுவுயிர்: the numbers seem to count the breaths a life spends, and the yoga asked for would make the breath return (மீளும்படி). Whether they add up to the traditional daily count of breaths is a guess. The plea is in the language of Saiva Siddhanta (பசுபாசத் தேகம், இருவினை).

links.note: Tirumular asks what men gain by arguing when time slips away, since arguers cannot bow at the Stainless one's feet; 1028 sends those who learn books to quarrel to Death's town with those who do not melt for the Lord.
The Naladiyar's hoarder who neither enjoys nor gives dies mocked by his own wealth; 1028 adds that such men, who seek money and live without giving, go to Death's town.

Two songs of the same refrain-set turn on disease: 1025 asks for the feet at the hour when humoral disease brings death, 1027 lists diseases at length and asks to be kept from them and set in release.

source_issues: 1022: பாயற் கிநட்முழ்கிப் is garbled (perhaps பாயற்கிடை மூழ்கி).
1023, 1025, 1034: the glyph ஡ stands for ஊ (களிறூரும், உடலூடே, குடிலூடே).
1033: initial உ is split from its word by a space (உ ழலாதே).
